name.hi: हर वर्कआउट से पहले 200 मिलीग्राम कैफीन

dose: 200 mg caffeine (one pre-workout scoop, two strong coffees, or a 200 mg tablet) taken 30–60 minutes before training, daily. Roughly 3 mg per kg for a 65 kg person.

summary.en: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors in the brain, so the 'tired' signal is muted and dopamine and adrenaline run a little higher. At 3 mg/kg it reliably improves endurance, power output and perceived effort by a few percent, and shortens reaction time. Its half-life is about 5 hours, so a late-afternoon dose is still half-active at bedtime, and daily use builds tolerance to the buzz within 1–2 weeks while most of the performance benefit remains.
summary.hi: कैफीन दिमाग़ में एडेनोसिन रिसेप्टर को ब्लॉक करता है, जिससे थकान का सिग्नल दब जाता है और डोपामिन-एड्रेनालिन थोड़ा ऊपर रहता है। 200 मिलीग्राम पर सहनशक्ति, ताक़त और मेहनत का अहसास कुछ प्रतिशत बेहतर होता है। इसकी हाफ़-लाइफ़ करीब 5 घंटे है, इसलिए शाम की डोज़ सोते वक़्त भी आधी असरदार रहती है। रोज़ लेने से 1–2 हफ़्ते में 'किक' कम हो जाती है, पर परफ़ॉर्मेंस का फ़ायदा काफ़ी हद तक बना रहता है।

indian_context: A cup of Indian chai has ~30–50 mg caffeine and filter coffee ~80–120 mg, so someone drinking 3–4 cups a day plus a 200 mg pre-workout can quietly cross 400 mg. Indian pre-workout powders often stack caffeine with yohimbine, synephrine or undeclared stimulants; FSSAI caps caffeine at 300 mg/L in energy drinks but supplement powders are loosely policed. Evening gym slots (7–9 PM) are the norm in Indian cities, which puts the dose right where it damages sleep most.
sources: Guest NS et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: caffeine and exercise performance. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021
EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products. Scientific Opinion on the safety of caffeine. EFSA Journal. 2015
Drake C et al. Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. J Clin Sleep Med. 2013
Juliano LM, Griffiths RR. A critical review of caffeine withdrawal. Psychopharmacology. 2004
caution: Keep total daily caffeine under 400 mg (200 mg if pregnant). Avoid if you have uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmia, panic disorder or severe reflux. Take it at least 6–8 hours before bed. Do not stack with other stimulants. Stopping abruptly after daily use causes 1–3 days of headache and fatigue; taper instead.

timeline.headline: Peak in 45 min: alert, faster, heart rate up, pupils wide

effects.note: Caffeine crosses into the brain and blocks adenosine A1/A2A receptors within 30–60 minutes. Perceived effort drops, reaction time shortens and you push harder in the session.
Adrenaline release rises, mobilising fatty acids and glucose for fuel. Useful for the workout, but it is a stress hormone response and it is why hands may shake.
Heart rate and systolic blood pressure rise for 2–3 hours in someone not used to caffeine. In healthy adults this is transient and harmless.
Caffeine increases calcium release in muscle fibres and lowers the sense of fatigue, giving a small but consistent boost to strength-endurance and power output.
With a ~5 hour half-life, 200 mg at 6 PM leaves ~100 mg active at 11 PM. Melatonin release is delayed and deep sleep is cut even when you fall asleep fine.

metric.label: Sleep loss if taken 6 h before bed

timeline.headline: Tolerance starting; sleep debt quietly builds

effects.note: The brain responds to daily blockade by making more adenosine receptors. The buzz fades but the performance benefit is largely preserved in trials even in habitual users.
If the dose is taken in the evening, a week of shortened deep sleep already blunts memory consolidation and next-day recovery; morning dosing avoids this entirely.
Caffeine raises gastric acid output and relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter, so reflux or a sour stomach is common on an empty-stomach dose.
A mild diuretic effect appears in non-users but disappears with daily use; net fluid balance stays normal within days.

timeline.headline: Full tolerance to the buzz; dependence begins

effects.note: Receptor upregulation is complete. Skipping a day now brings withdrawal within 12–24 hours: headache, heaviness, poor concentration. The workout benefit persists but the 'edge' feels smaller.
The blood pressure spike shrinks with tolerance; resting BP and heart rate in daily users are close to non-users.
A month of slightly harder sessions is real training volume in the bank; the effect on performance in tolerant users is smaller but still measurable in most studies.

timeline.headline: Stable state; the sleep timing decides whether it helps or hurts

effects.note: Morning or early-afternoon users are in a clean steady state: reliable pre-training lift, normal sleep. Evening users are running on a chronic 30–60 minute nightly sleep deficit, which slowly cancels the training gains.
Cortisol response to caffeine diminishes with habitual use; 'adrenal fatigue' is not a recognised condition, but poor sleep from late dosing does raise evening cortisol.
Caffeine causes a small increase in urinary calcium (~5 mg per 100 mg caffeine), trivial if dietary calcium is adequate; only a concern with very low calcium intake.

timeline.headline: Habit; withdrawal on rest days is the tell

effects.note: Physical dependence is established. Rest-day headache and irritability are caffeine withdrawal, not 'needing to train'. A 4–7 day break resets receptor numbers and restores the full effect.
Pre-workout drinks are acidic (citric/malic acid, pH ~3) and sipped over 30 minutes; enamel erosion over months is a dental problem, not a caffeine one. Rinse with water after.

The liver enzyme CYP1A2 clears caffeine; six months of daily use nudges it up slightly, so clearance gets a little faster. Regular coffee intake is associated with lower liver enzyme levels, not higher.

timeline.headline: A year in: no harm at this dose for healthy adults

effects.note: Habitual caffeine up to ~400 mg/day is not linked to hypertension, atrial fibrillation or heart attack in large cohorts; if anything moderate coffee drinkers do slightly better.
Cognitive benefit is mostly reversal of withdrawal; the true net gain over a non-user is small. Anxiety-prone people are the exception and often feel steadily worse.
The compounded benefit is the extra training quality across a year. The ergogenic effect is genuine, but it is worth a few percent, not a transformation.

timeline.headline: Five years: safe habit if timed well; watch the stack, not the caffeine

effects.note: Long-term moderate caffeine is associated with lower risk of Parkinson's disease and possibly dementia in cohort studies; causation is not proven, but there is no signal of harm.

At 200–400 mg/day, no long-term cardiovascular harm in healthy adults. The real 5-year risk in the pre-workout world is the other stimulants in the tub, which have caused hypertension, arrhythmias and liver injury.
For evening trainers, five years of clipped deep sleep is the one true cumulative cost: worse recovery, mood and metabolic health. Moving the dose before 2 PM removes it.
